newsitem.title: USA: Clinton aides discuss military strike on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Clinton aides discuss military strike on Iraq.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's senior national security advisers met on Friday to map out his next moves in a showdown with Iraq as more U.S. ships and warplanes moved into position to strike when Clinton is ready.

With those strikes treated as a foregone conclusion around Washington -- not whether but when and what -- White House officials said Clinton would not be rushed and was taking time to try to build support among reluctant allies and the public.

"He wants to build a consensus. It's important," one official said in noting that the president was willing to defer an immediate strike briefly in order to strengthen its diplomatic and political underpinnings.

As the spadework proceeded, a U.S. military buildup in the Gulf region continued as well. Eight sleek, radar-dodging stealth warplanes arrived in Kuwait and a second U.S. aircraft carrier steamed toward the Suez Canal en route to the Gulf.

The crisis strategy session led by Secretary of State Warren Christopher, Defense Secretary William Perry and White House National Security Adviser Anthony Lake did not include Clinton, but officials said it was called to develop options for him in the clash with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

If Iraq's leader "continues his provocations he should be aware of the fact that the United States has a lot of options and I suspect that President Clinton will exercise those in the next few days," Senator Sam Nunn, a Georgia Democrat and a an influential voice on national security issues, told CNN.

"Saddam needs to recognize that in the next go-around we're probably going to hit supply depots, logistics, communications -- all of those are legitimate targets -- command and control, as well as headquarters," Nunn said.

With the specter of campaign politics looming over every decision Clinton makes between now and the November 5 election, he has been trying to build support among allies -- many of whom opposed initial U.S. cruise missile strikes at Iraq last week -- and American voters for this showdown.
"There has been extensive consultation on this" with allies, said Deputy Press Secretary Mary Ellen Glynn. "The president has made some phone calls."

With the exception of the British, most allies have been tepid at best in their support for the two cruise missile attacks Clinton ordered last week in retaliation for military action by Baghdad against Kurds in the north.

Since then, Iraqi forces have fired on American warplanes patrolling the no-fly zones in both northern and southern Iraq and efforts have been made by Baghdad to repair some of the southern air defense batteries damaged in the missile attack.
Clinton's determination to strike back continued to spark political rumblings at home as well as misgivings abroad.
Senator Kay Bailey Hutchison, a Texas Republican, echoed general criticism from her party that Democrat Clinton has not sufficiently explained his Iraq policy.

"Before we haul off ansd start escalating the bombing, which we may need to do, we need to know what the president's endgame is and he has not come to Congress and he has not consulted with the American people," she said on CNN.

With Perry suggesting the United States will retaliate in a "disproportionate" way, Washington has been massing a major strike force in the region, including warships and bombers armed with cruise missiles and jet attack planes.

A Pentagon official said the eight F-117A stealth fighters, designed to drop laser-guided bombs while avoiding Iraqi radar, arrived in Kuwait from the United States on Friday after a 20-hour non-stop flight.

Four U.S. B-52 bombers with cruise missiles have already rebased to the Indian Ocean island of Diego Garcia, and the aircraft carrier Enterprise was steaming south in the Mediterranean en route to the Gulf with some 75 warplanes. The carrier Carl Vinson is already on patrol there.
Navy officials said the Enterprise would pass through Suez into the Red Sea this weekend.

The Army announced on Thursday that it was moving two Patriot anti-missile batteries to the Gulf region with about 150 soldiers. Defense officials said privately they would go to Saudi Arabia. Patriot missiles were used as a defense against Iraqi Scud missiles during the 1991 Gulf War.
